articles.title: A new PBS documentary shows the intensity and heart behind the Joffrey Ballet's ‘Winning Works’ competition
articles.description:
A new documentary captures the discipline, creativity and heart behind the Joffrey Ballet’s trailblazing “Winning Works” program for emerging artists
historically excluded from ballet.

“Joffrey Ballet: The Next Movement” premieres Friday at 9 p.m. Eastern (8 p.m. Central) on PBS, PBS.org and the PBS app. The film was produced by Chicago-based Kartemquin Films and directed by South Sider Cam Be. It follows five choreographers over two weeks as they prepare new works featuring students from Joffrey’s Grainger Academy.

The piece not only highlights the intensity of staging performances, but the personal stories of the BIPOC artists, many of whom have had to pave their own way in an art form that has, until recent years, mostly featured white dancers and choreographers.

“I want you to understand the level of dedication it takes and the work these choreographers went through to get to the spaces they’re in,” said Cam Be, 44, of Bronzeville.

“But also, I want you to understand that they’re just human beings, and that they have life experiences and trauma that they’ve had to deal with, and they continue to push through.”

The film features choreographers who competed for slots in the 14th annual “Winning Works” showcase, which took place in March 2024. They include Manoela Gonçalves, of Rio de Janeiro; Jainil Mehta, of Mumbai; Martha Nichols, of Brooklyn; Joffrey Ballet dancer Xavier Núñez, originally from Puerto Rico; and Houston Thomas, of Chicago.

Thomas’ story is an especially poignant part of the film, as he began as a student in the Joffrey Ballet’s outreach program and went on to dance professionally in Germany. His participation in “Winning Works” marked his return to Chicago for the first time since his mother died.

His ballet, “Dear Chicago: A Love Letter,” will also be performed by the Joffrey Ballet as part of the “Notes on Love” program in February.

“It was a bit of an emotional homecoming for him,” Be said. “But also a triumphant story of fulfilling his dream as a dancer and now being a choreographer.”

The film also includes plenty of behind-the-scenes drama, from performers navigating the two-week time crunch and injuries to working with unconventional props and learning challenging dance styles.

“There's layers of conflict just in terms of putting the dance together,” Be said.
“I hope [viewers] feel like they’re in the wardrobe room helping with the costumes, or that they are in the room practicing with the dancers.”

As a Black director facing barriers in his own industry, Be said he related to the choreographers.

“I think the ‘Winning Works’ program is a foot in the door,” he said. “It’s starting the process. And, hopefully, the film creates a larger conversation to push for more opportunities for people of color, and specifically Black people and women.”

Above all, Be said he hopes the documentary motivates each person watching, even if they are new to ballet.

“I hope that the audience can find the level of inspiration in their own lives to push for something that they want to do as well,” he said.

The Joffrey is among the Chicago arts organizations that participated in a 2025 WBEZ/Sun-Times survey on diversity in leadership of top cultural groups.

Leadership said the ballet company plans to forge ahead with its diversity, equity and inclusion plans and programming, even as the Trump administration criticizes and cuts arts funding for such efforts.

articles.title: Ed Sheeran has 10 U.S. shows left — and no backing band or opening acts
articles.description: The fate of Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour is suddenly uncertain after all of the British singer's remaining opening acts quit in solidarity with the rapper Macklemore, who was dropped from the remaining North American dates over pro-Palestinian comments. Hours after Sheeran released a statement saying it was the promoter's decision to remove Macklemore from the tour and not his, the rest of his supporting acts — Irish singer Aaron Rowe, Danish pop band Lukas Graham and songwriter Finneas — as well as Sheeran's house band, Beoga, announced that they were pulling out in protest. "Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed," Finneas, the brother of Billie Eilish, wrote in a note posted to Instagram . "I have decided to withdraw from my upcoming tour dates with Ed Sheeran. I stand with Palestine and its people." The Irish artists cited their country's history of oppression in their decisions to drop out. "I don't take the decision lightly. Ed has been a friend to me and has changed my life, I could never thank him enough for this," Rowe wrote in his own Instagram post . "But as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation. I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up against Israeli genocide and who highlight the savage murder of children." "We are Irish people who understand colonialism," Beoga said in a statement on Instagram . "As founding members of the Irish Artists for Palestine movement, we are committed activists for justice and will continue to be." Finneas O'Connell attends the Grammy Awards in Los Angeles on Feb. 1. John Shearer/Getty Images for The Recording Academy Finneas was scheduled to be the supporting act for stops in Chile, Paraguay, Argentina and Brazil. Rowe and Lukas Graham had been due to open for Sheeran on his remaining 11 North American tour dates. As of Wednesday, they were all still listed as supporting acts on Sheeran's Loop Tour website . Remaining dates of Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour Sept. 19: Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia Sept. 25-26: Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Mass. Oct. 3: Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta Oct. 10: Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis Oct. 17: Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, N.C. Oct. 24: AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas Oct 29-30: Seminole Hard Rock Hotel & Casino in Hollywood, Fla. Nov 7: Raymond James Stadium in Tampa Nov. 21-22: Estadio Bicentenario De La Florida in Santiago, Chile Nov. 26: Nueva Olla Stadium in Asunción, Paraguay Nov. 29: Tomás Adolfo Ducó Stadium (Huracán Stadium) in Buenos Aires, Argentina Dec. 5-6: Nubank Parque in Sao Paulo Dec. 11: Estadio Ciudad de los Deportes in Mexico City None of the U.S. shows are sold out. It's unclear whether ticket holders who may also want to protest in solidarity with Macklemore can exchange their tickets or get a refund. According to Ticketmaster , event organizers determine refund policies, and they are "only allowed in limited circumstances." Ticketmaster's standard purchase policy states : "Opening Acts are subject to change or cancellation at any time without notice. No refund will be given due to a change in or cancellation of a Participant or Opening Act." And according to Sheeran's website , all sales are final: "If you change your mind about your ticket purchase, you are not entitled to a refund or exchange on your ticket purchase." How we got here Macklemore performs in Dublin in 2025. Kieran Frost/Redferns via Getty Images Earlier this month, Macklemore performed as Sheeran's opening act at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, where he made pro-Palestinian comments and performed his protest song "Hind's Hall." The song was written after protests in support of Palestine occurred on college campuses across the U.S. in 2024, and is named after Hind Rajab, a 5-year-old Palestinian girl who was killed by Israeli troops in Gaza. Last month, Israel's military acknowledged that its troops had opened fire on the car carrying Hind and her family and said it had opened a criminal investigation into the killing. "A big part of the ​reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could ​stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free ‌Palestine,'" ⁠Macklemore said onstage at MetLife Stadium. "To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters, criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, it in no way is criticism of you," the rapper added. His comments drew criticism from pop singer Pink and pro-Israel groups, including the Israeli-American Council, which started a petition to have the Grammy-winning artist dropped from the tour. Robert Kraft speaks to the media at Tom Brady's induction into the New England Patriots Hall of Fame in Foxborough, Mass., in 2024. Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Robert Kraft, owner of the NFL's New England Patriots, said in a statement that Macklemore wouldn't be welcome at Gillette Stadium for the tour's scheduled performances at the end of September. According to Macklemore , Kraft — who in 2024 withdrew funding for Columbia University over its handling of protests against Israel's war in Gaza — had "rallied some of the other stadium owners" to give Sheeran "an ultimatum: If Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play." In his statement , Sheeran said that he had spoken with Kraft and the other venues "to try and build a bridge," but that their "decision was final." "After Macklemore's performances at my New Jersey shows, venues on my upcoming tour dates communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting," he said on Instagram Tuesday. "Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine." View this post on Instagram The promoter, Messina Touring Group, said in a statement to Rolling Stone that it had been notified by venues on Sheeran's upcoming U.S. tour that they would "not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup, which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans." The company said that "after discussions with stakeholders," it decided to remove Macklemore. Representatives for the Messina Touring Group did not immediately return a request for comment. In his Instagram post, Sheeran also insisted that "I do not use my professional platform for politics." "My audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds," he said. "Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum." But several commenters were quick to point out that Sheeran has, in fact, used his professional platform to support political causes , including a video he posted ahead of his performance at a 2022 benefit concert for Ukraine. "I just wanted to say to all Ukrainians, I love you, I stand with you, and I'm so proud to be playing this fundraising event," he said. On Wednesday, Macklemore pledged to donate $1 million from the net earnings from Ed Sheeran's tour to organizations that support Palestinians. The rapper then called on Kraft to match his donation.
